newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivory Coast's Essy says U.N. must pay its way.
newsitem.headline: Ivory Coast's Essy says U.N. must pay its way.

text.p: Ivory Coast Foreign Minister Amara Essy, a frontrunner for the top job at the United Nations, has said the world body must live within its means but at the same time member states have to pay their dues.
Essy told Reuters late on Tuesday that if he was elected to succeed Boutros Boutros-Ghali as U.N. secretary-general he would launch a review to stamp out duplication in the world body.
But he denied he would scrap any of the world body's mainstream institutions such as the U.N. Industrial Development Organisation UNIDO, as earlier reported by Reuters.
"You cannot spend what you don't have," Essy said by telephone, but he added that the onus was on member states to ensure their contributions were up to date.
Some members, given the development of their economies, could perhaps afford to pay more, he said, speaking in French.

Essy, who finished in second place to Ghana's Kofi Annan in an informal U.N. Security Council ballot on Tuesday, called for streamlining of the world body's bureaucracy and internal organisation to focus its resources on development.
"A study must be conducted to see where there is duplication," he said. "My idea is that we are in a world that is in constant evolution. A reform can never be static... Reform is a continuous task."
He told reporters in Ivory Coast's commercial capital Abidjan earlier on Tuesday he had already started efforts at reform when he was president of the U.N. General Assembly.

Essy, one of four African candidates nominated by their governments on Friday, was Ivory Coast's permanent U.N. representative from 1981 to 1990. He presided over the general assembly's 49th annual session in the year to September 1995.
He said Boutros-Ghali had cut staff numbers from 12,000 in 1994 to 8,500 in 1995 but added that a major problem was unpaid membership dues. "Up until now there has been a huge deficit."
Egypt's Boutros-Ghali has temporarily set aside his bid for the traditional second term as secretary-general in the face of a U.S. veto.

The United States says Boutros-Ghali has not done enough to reform the world body but that Africa should still have the right to the second five-year term. Ghana, Ivory Coast, Niger and Mauritania have nominated nationals for the post.
To win, a candidate needs at least nine votes in the 15-seat Security Council and no veto from any of its five permanent members -- the United States, Russia, China, Britain and France.
Annan, under-secretary general in charge of peacekeeping, received 10 votes in favour but one of four votes against him came from a permanent member -- believed to be France.
Essy received seven votes in favour but two of the four votes against him were from permanent members.
Any candidate approved by the council must be endorsed by the 185-member General Assembly before December 31 when Boutros-Ghali's five-year term expires.
